newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: INTERVIEW - Chrysler's Lutz sees internal growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Chrysler's Lutz sees internal growth.

text.p: Chrysler Corp vice chairman Robert Lutz said on Monday the U.S. carmaker has no intention of boosting its international presence through acquisitions or by setting up more European production sites like its rivals.

Lutz told Reuters in an interview that Chrysler instead wants to "grow organically" and build on its reputation as a small but profitable carmaker and not follow the lead of General Motors Corp and Ford Motor Co by acquiring a foreign carmaker or by buying or establishing new factories.

"We believe our strategy of exporting products primarily from the U.S. is the best use of capital and is the least risk and the highest profitable way for us to grow internationally," said Lutz, in Switzerland to attend the Geneva car show.

Lutz said that 10 to 15 years ago Chrysler would have considered acquisitions but it now sought internal growth, noting the almost doubling of Chrysler's production to three million units a year from 1991 to 1996.
"We do not want to become a mass producer and establish a large asset base in Europe," Lutz said in the interview after a speech to the American International Club of Geneva.
"One of our advantages is that we are small and flexible but that we do not have large plants in Europe," he said. "Why do that to ourselves when others wish they didn't have all that."

Chrysler, which has some $7.5 billion in reserves, has been under pressure to step up its international presence and has long been mentioned as a possible takeover candidate by several of the remaining independent European carmakers that would become a bridgehead to launch an international expansion.

The No. 3 U.S. carmaker is dwarfed in Europe and elsewhere by Ford and GM but both carmakers have been suffering losses or struggling to turn a profit due to intense competition in a European market that analysts say is becoming saturated.
Chrysler sold 222,035 cars into international markets last year, setting a new record and topping by nearly 20 percent the old mark in 1995 of 185,934 vehicles.

"Wall Street has finally begun to realise that our strategy may well be the correct way," said Lutz, who throttled back on his corporate responsibilities after turning 65 in February by giving up his title as president and chief operating officer.

"They have stopped confusing size with quality or the ability to create shareholder value. We are demonstrating that our way works and provides stable growth in earnings and shareholder value," he said.
Lutz said Chrysler would expand its production capabilities at a plant in Graz, Austria, where Chrysler builds mini-vans and Jeep vehicles for sales in Europe as well as Asia.
The Graz facility, which can produce up to 75,000 minivans a year and another 70,000 of the popular Jeep vehicles, is currently producing about 100,000 vehicles a year.
But Lutz said Chrysler had no immediate plans to reach full production levels, which would require a three-shift operation.
Chrysler sells vehicles into more than 140 countries outside its main markets in the United States, Canada and Mexico.

The carmaker has been riding on the success of its minivans, which saw sales in 1995 rise 21 percent to 52,530 vehicles. The introduction of right-hand-drive minivans in the coming months should also add to the growth, Chrysler has said.
